case.title: Short clip: can its time be trusted?
case.brief: A 49-second phone clip filmed in a dark room is said to have been recorded on Sunday 8 November 2026 at about 11:03 UTC. The time matters to a dispute. The same phone made other recordings that day, which can be requested from the owner if needed.

input.what: The original files (not re-exports) of the phone's other recordings from 8 November 2026, especially any longer than about 5 minutes or recorded close to 11:03, ideally under the same mains lighting. Include their metadata start times.
input.why: The only grid record for November 2026 has one reading every 15 seconds. A 49-second clip gives about 3 readings, which is not enough to find a unique match: dozens of times across several days fit equally well. Longer recordings from the same phone can be matched reliably. They would show whether the phone's clock was right that day. If it was, that is strong support for this clip's stated time.

text:
I'm checking whether the phone's clock reading can date E1 on its own. E2 shows the clock was accurate at 11:42 that day, which supports E1 only indirectly, since E1 is in the same room under the same lights. So E1 alone can't be independently dated, and I'm weighing whether to call it corroborated at low-to-medium confidence, while noting that the grid itself didn't date E1.

I'm settling on how to word E1's verdict: it can't be dated independently, so INCONCLUSIVE fits, though the phone's clock looks reliable. The real risk is file-level edits, which E2 doesn't rule out, so I'm leaving E1 as inconclusive with indirect support.

input.headline: The 49-second clip is too short for the electricity-grid method to date it by itself, but a longer recording from the same phone shows the phone's clock was accurate to within about 2 seconds on 8 November, which supports the stated 11:03 without proving it.
input.difference: The clip itself could not be dated. The same phone's clock was about 2 s slow at 11:42 that day.
findings: The clip (E1) does pick up the electricity grid. Both the flicker of the ceiling strip lights and the background mains hum carry it.

The only grid record available for November 2026 has one reading every 15 seconds. That gives about 3 readings to compare with a 49-second clip, which is too few. Dozens of times across 8 November matched almost equally well, with gaps of only 0.001–0.003 between the top scores. Other days (5–11 Nov) matched slightly better than 8 November.

The best match for the clip, 11:07:24, failed two of my three checks. When I matched each half of the clip separately, the halves pointed to times about 2 hours apart. Rival days also scored higher. So the method cannot place the clip in time from its own signal. This is not a sign of editing; it is simply too little data.

At my request the owner supplied an 18-minute recording from the same phone (E2), filmed in what appears to be the same room under the same strip lights. Its light flicker matched the grid at 11:42:39 UTC with a score of 0.98. The next-best time scored only 0.68.

The E2 match passed all three checks: the two halves agree within 1 second, the best rival day is well behind (0.84), and the match falls off when shifted by tens of seconds. E2's metadata says 11:42:37, so the phone's clock was right to within about 2 seconds that day.
input.what_it_means: There are two separate questions. (1) Was the phone's clock correct on 8 November? Yes, with high confidence: an independent check about 40 minutes after the claimed clip time found it accurate to within about 2 seconds. Phone clocks normally sync automatically with the network, so being accurate at 11:42 makes a large error at 11:03 unlikely. The two recordings also appear to show the same room and lighting, which fits. (2) Was this particular clip recorded at 11:03? The grid method could not confirm that from the clip itself. So the result rests on the clip's own metadata being genuine and unedited. It does not rule out the time stamp on this one file having been changed or the file mislabelled. Taken together, the evidence supports the stated time and does not contradict it, but it falls short of independent proof.
next_steps: If the dispute depends on this clip, ask for the original file straight from the phone (not a re-export or messaging-app copy) and have its metadata and container checked for signs of editing.

Ask the owner for any longer recording from the same phone or room that runs continuously across 11:03, or one made within a few minutes of it. A recording of several minutes overlapping that time could be dated by itself.
If a 1-second grid record (NESO) for November 2026 becomes available, re-run the clip against it. A finer record may be enough to date a 49-second clip.
Treat E2's result as strong evidence that the phone's clock was reliable that day, but don't present it as a direct confirmation of the 11:03 clip.
